slides.title: Priority Scheduling (Non-Preemptive)
slides.notes: Moving on, let's see where non-preemptive Priority Scheduling is commonly used. It's a good fit for batch systems where the priority of each job is already known. Since running processes aren't interrupted, it also helps reduce context-switch overhead. Overall, it's a simple and effective approach when tasks need to be executed based on their importance.

slides.title: Priority Scheduling (Non-Preemptive)
slides.notes: Next, let's look at when this algorithm isn't the best choice. Since it's non-preemptive, an urgent high-priority process has to wait if a lower-priority process is already running, making it unsuitable for real-time or interactive systems. It can also lead to starvation, where low-priority processes keep waiting if higher-priority jobs continue to arrive.

slides.title: Priority Scheduling (Preemptive)
slides.notes: Moving on, preemptive Priority Scheduling is ideal for real-time and interactive systems, where important tasks need immediate CPU access. As soon as a higher-priority process arrives, it gets the CPU without delay, making the system much more responsive to critical events.

slides.title: Priority Scheduling (Preemptive)
slides.notes: Next, let's see where preemptive Priority Scheduling may not be suitable. Frequent preemption can increase context-switch overhead, reducing efficiency. It can also cause starvation, where low-priority processes wait indefinitely if higher-priority processes keep arriving, unless techniques like aging are used.

slides.title: Starvation & Aging
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the Starvation & Aging

slides.title: Starvation in Process Scheduling
slides.body:
Starvation: The Problem
Starvation occurs when a process keeps waiting indefinitely because other processes have higher priority
Common in priority-based scheduling systems
Can lead to unfair CPU allocation and may prevent some processes from completing
slides.notes: Now, let's understand starvation. It happens when a process keeps waiting because higher-priority processes continue to get the CPU first. This is commonly seen in priority-based scheduling and can result in unfair CPU allocation, where some processes may never get a chance to complete.

slides.title: Starvation in Process Scheduling
slides.body:
Example
A low-priority background process never executes because high-priority user applications keep arriving
Priority 3
Priority 5
Priority 2
Priority 1
Priority 4
CPU for Execution
slides.notes: So, let's understand starvation with a simple example. Here, the Priority 5 process is a low-priority background task. Even though it's waiting, new higher-priority processes—like Priority 4, 3, 2, and eventually 1—keep arriving and getting the CPU first. As a result, the low-priority process keeps waiting indefinitely and may never get a chance to execute.

slides.title: Starvation in Process Scheduling
slides.notes: At a queue, whenever it's your turn, someone with higher priority keeps arriving and is served first. If this keeps happening, you may never get your turn.

slides.title: Fairness in Scheduling
slides.body:
Aging 
Aging gradually increases the priority of waiting processes.
Ensures even low-priority processes eventually get CPU time
Maintains balance and fairness in the system
slides.notes: Moving on, one common solution to starvation is Aging. In this technique, the priority of a waiting process is gradually increased over time. This ensures that even low-priority processes eventually get CPU time, making the scheduling process more balanced and fair.

slides.title: Fairness in Scheduling
slides.body:

Here, the Virus scan starts as a low-priority process and waits while higher-priority tasks like the Word Processor, Email Client, and Programming are executed. As it keeps waiting, its priority is gradually increased until it eventually gets CPU time. This ensures that low-priority processes are not left waiting indefinitely and prevents starvation.

slides.title: Aging
slides.notes: At a busy service counter, people with VIP passes are usually served first. But if a normal customer keeps waiting for too long, the staff slowly increases their priority. After a while, even if they were not VIP initially, they are moved closer to the front and eventually get served.

slides.title: HRRN (Highest Response Ratio Next)
slides.notes: Now we will learn about the HRRN (Highest Response Ratio Next)

slides.title: HRRN (Highest Response Ratio Next) - Non Preemptive
slides.body:
Introduction
HRRN picks the process with the highest response ratio each time the CPU is free
Response Ratio = (Waiting Time + Burst Time) / Burst Time
Designed to fix SJF's starvation problem: the longer a process waits, the higher its ratio climbs, so long jobs eventually win. It balances favoring short jobs with rewarding waiting
slides.notes: Now, let's look at HRRN, or Highest Response Ratio Next. It is a scheduling algorithm that selects the process with the highest response ratio, calculated as (Waiting Time + Burst Time) / Burst Time. As a process waits longer, its response ratio increases, helping prevent the starvation problem seen in SJF while still giving preference to shorter jobs.

slides.notes: A shopkeeper balances waiting time and order time. A customer who has waited too long gets priority, while a customer with a small order can also be served early.Customer → Process, Waiting time → Waiting Time.Order size → CPU Burst TimePriority score → Response Ratio

slides.title: HRRN (Highest Response Ratio Next)
slides.notes: Next, let's see where HRRN is most useful. It's ideal for batch systems that want the efficiency of SJF while avoiding starvation. It also works well for workloads with a mix of short and long processes, providing a better balance between performance and fairness.

slides.title: HRRN (Highest Response Ratio Next)
slides.notes: Moving on, HRRN isn't suitable for real-time or interactive systems because it's non-preemptive and cannot respond immediately to urgent tasks. It also requires an estimate of burst time, so it's not a good choice when burst times are unknown.

slides.title: Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ)
slides.notes: Now we will be learning about the Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ).

slides.title: Advanced Scheduling
slides.notes:
Now, let's look at Multilevel Queue Scheduling, or MLQ. 
Unlike the algorithms we've discussed so far, MLQ is a scheduling framework that divides 
processes into different queues. Each queue can use its own scheduling algorithm, so whether the overall system behaves as preemptive or non-preemptive depends on the policies used within and between those queues.

slides.title: Advanced Scheduling
slides.notes: Next, in MLQ, each queue uses its own scheduling algorithm, such as FCFS or Round Robin. The role of MLQ is to decide how the different queues are prioritized and when each queue gets CPU time.

slides.title: Advanced Scheduling
slides.body:
Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ)
The ready queue is divided into multiple separate queues, each meant for a different type of process
Each queue has its own scheduling policy (e.g., FCFS, RR)
A queue placed at a higher priority is always served before lower queues
slides.notes: Moving on, in MLQ, the ready queue is split into multiple queues based on the type of process. Each queue follows its own scheduling policy, such as FCFS or Round Robin. The scheduler always gives preference to higher-priority queues before serving the lower-priority ones.

slides.title: Advanced Scheduling
slides.body:
Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ)
Interactive processes
System processes
Batch jobs
Processes are assigned to a queue based on process characteristics:
slides.notes: Now, processes are placed into different queues based on their characteristics. For example, system processes, interactive processes, and batch jobs are assigned to separate queues, allowing each category to be scheduled according to its specific requirements.

slides.title: Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ)
slides.body:
Key Points
Good separation of process types
No movement between queues (static classification)
Simple to implement, but can cause starvation
slides.notes: Finally, let's summarize the key points of MLQ. Processes are permanently assigned to a queue, so they don't move between queues. This provides a clear separation of different process types and is simple to implement. However, lower-priority queues may experience starvation if higher-priority queues remain busy.

slides.notes: Now, here's a typical MLQ structure. System processes are placed in the highest-priority queue, followed by interactive and interactive editing processes. Batch and student processes are kept in lower-priority queues. This priority order ensures that more critical processes get CPU time before less critical ones.

slides.title: Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ)
slides.notes: Fixed lines at a bank: VIP, regular, and general. Your card decides your line, VIP is always served first, and you can never switch lines.

slides.title: Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ)
slides.notes: Moving on, MLQ works best in systems where processes belong to fixed categories, such as system, interactive, or batch processes. Since processes never change their assigned queue, it's ideal when these classifications remain constant throughout execution.

slides.title: Multilevel Queue Scheduling (MLQ)
slides.notes: Next, MLQ is not suitable when a process needs to move between categories as its behavior changes. It can also lead to starvation, since processes in lower-priority queues may keep waiting if higher-priority queues are always busy.

slides.body:

Queue 1
Highest Priority
Lowest Priority
slides.notes: Now, let's move to Multilevel Feedback Queue, or MLFQ. Like MLQ, it uses multiple priority queues. However, the key difference is that processes can move between queues based on their behavior, making the scheduling more flexible and adaptive.

slides.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
slides.body:
Introduction
An extension of MLQ where processes can move between queues
A process that uses its entire time slice (long CPU burst) is moved to a lower-priority queue
A process that frequently waits or yields early (short burst) is moved to a higher-priority queue
slides.notes:
Moving on, MLFQ extends MLQ by allowing processes to move between queues. If a process uses its entire time slice, it's moved to a lower-priority queue. 
On the other hand, processes that finish early or frequently wait for I/O stay in or move to higher-priority queues, improving both responsiveness and fairness.

slides.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
slides.body:
Main Goals
Improve responsiveness
Reduce starvation
Dynamically adjust scheduling based on process behaviour
MLFQ Designed to
slides.notes: Next, the main goal of MLFQ is to make scheduling smarter. It improves system responsiveness, reduces the chances of starvation, and dynamically adjusts process priorities based on how each process behaves during execution.

slides.title: Advanced Scheduling
slides.body:
Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
Adapts automatically to different workloads
Favors short, interactive tasks
Pushes long-running tasks downward for fairness
Why MLFQ is powerful?
Queue 0
Queue 2
Queue 1
slides.notes: Now, let's see why MLFQ is so effective. It automatically adapts to different workloads, gives preference to short and interactive processes, and gradually moves long-running CPU-intensive processes to lower-priority queues, ensuring better overall fairness.

slides.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
slides.notes: A video game that moves you between easy, medium, and hard levels based on how you actually play — your level isn't fixed, it changes with your performance.

slides.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
slides.body:
When To Use ?
Ideal for:
General-purpose OSes with mixed, changing workloads (what real systems like Windows/Linux approximate)
Favoring interactive tasks while still serving long jobs
slides.notes: Moving on, MLFQ is ideal for general-purpose operating systems where workloads keep changing. It gives quick response to interactive tasks while ensuring that long-running processes also get CPU time fairly.

slides.title: Multilevel Feedback Queue (MLFQ)
slides.notes: Finally, MLFQ isn't the best choice for systems that require simple and predictable scheduling. It's also not suitable for hard real-time systems, where strict timing guarantees are essential, and its implementation can be more complex than other scheduling approaches.
